howto.name: How to prepare for the Colorado Chatbot Safety Act

steps.name: Decide whether your chatbot is covered
steps.text: List every conversational AI product your organisation offers to Colorado residents and test each against the Act's definitions and exemptions. A customer-service bot and a companion app are treated differently; the proposed rules draw the line.

steps.name: Build age estimation and disclosure into the product
steps.text: The Act requires a reasonable method of estimating whether a user is a minor and a clear disclosure that the user is talking to an AI. Design both into the onboarding flow now, with a record of how each decision was reached.

steps.name: Write the self-harm protocol
steps.text: Operators must have a protocol for conversations that raise suicide or self-harm, including referral to crisis resources. Write it, test it against sample conversations, and keep the test record.

steps.name: Plan the annual report
steps.text: The Act requires annual reporting to the Attorney General. Decide who owns the report, what it counts, and how the counts are produced from logs you already keep.

steps.name: Follow the rulemaking
steps.text: The Attorney General's rules for this Act come from the same proceeding as the ADMT Act rules: hearing October 26, 2026, comments to 11:59 p.m. MST that day. The final rules decide the detail of every step above.

body_html:
On this page

  • What the Chatbot Safety Act is
  • What it requires
  • The dates
  • How it fits with the ADMT Act

  • Sources

What the Colorado Chatbot Safety Act is

HB 26-1263, the Colorado Chatbot Safety Act, is Colorado's law for consumer-facing AI chatbots. It was passed in the 2026 session alongside SB 26-189, the Automated Decision-Making Technology Act, and the Attorney General is writing the rules for both in one proceeding. Its duties for operators apply from January 1, 2027.

Governor Polis signed HB 26-1263 into law on May 29, 2026, and it took effect on August 12, 2026. The source is the Colorado Legislative Council Staff final fiscal note for HB 26-1263 (July 13, 2026), which agrees with the LegiScan record of the bill. The Attorney General's AI rulemaking page gives July 1, 2026 as the signing date, which conflicts with the legislature's record. The Act does not require the Attorney General to make rules; the Attorney General has included it in the ADMT rulemaking voluntarily, mainly to define what the operator's annual report must contain.

What it requires

  • Age estimation. An operator must use a reasonable method to estimate whether a user is a minor.
  • AI disclosure. Users must be told, clearly, that they are interacting with an AI system and not a person.
  • Protections for teenage users. Additional duties apply to users the operator knows or estimates to be minors.
  • Suicide and self-harm protocols. An operator must have and follow a protocol for conversations that raise suicide or self-harm, including referral to crisis resources.
  • Annual reporting to the Attorney General. Operators report each year on the measures above and on what the protocols were used for.

The proposed rules filed on August 11, 2026 and the interim draft of October 6, 2026 give the detail: which chatbots are covered, what counts as a reasonable age estimate, and what the annual report contains. Until the rules are final, the Act's text is the floor and the proposed rules are the best guide to what the floor will mean.

The dates

January 1, 2027Operator duties apply

How it fits with the ADMT Act

SB 26-189 governs automated decision-making technology that materially influences a consequential decision about a consumer. HB 26-1263 governs the chatbot itself: what it tells the user, how it treats a minor, and what it does when a conversation turns to self-harm. A company can be covered by both, by one, or by neither, and the two sets of duties do not overlap. Our Colorado ADMT and Chatbot Safety Rulemaking page tracks the single proceeding that will produce the rules for both, and our Colorado AI Act page explains what SB 26-189 kept and removed from the repealed SB 24-205.

How to prepare

Decide whether each chatbot you offer in Colorado is covered. Build age estimation and the AI disclosure into onboarding, with a record of the method. Write and test the self-harm protocol. Decide who produces the annual report and from which logs. Then follow the rulemaking to the final text, because the rules decide the detail of every one of those steps.
